L172: # Destructuring
L173: 
L174: Baseline
L175: 
L176: Widely available
L177: 
L178: This feature is well established and works across many devices and browser versions. It’s been available across browsers since August 2016.
L179: 
L180:   * 【86†See full compatibility】
L181:   * 【87†Learn more】
L182: The destructuring syntax is a JavaScript syntax that makes it possible to unpack values from arrays, or properties from objects, into distinct variables. It can be used in locations that receive data (such as the left-hand side of an assignment or anywhere that creates new identifier bindings).
L183: ## In this article
L184: 
L185:   * 【88†Try it】
L186:   * 【89†Syntax】
L187:   * 【90†Description】
L188:   * 【91†Examples】
L189:   * 【92†Specifications】
L190:   * 【86†Browser compatibility】
L191:   * 【93†See also】
L192: 
L193: ## 【88†Try it】
L194: 
L195:     `let a, b, rest;
L196:     [a, b] = [10, 20];
L197: 
L198:     console.log(a);
L199:     // Expected output: 10
L200: 
L201:     console.log(b);
L202:     // Expected output: 20
L203: 
L204:     [a, b, ...rest] = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50];
L205: 
L206:     console.log(rest);
L207:     // Expected output: Array [30, 40, 50]
L208:     `
L209: ## 【89†Syntax】
L210: js
L211: 
L212:     `const [a, b] = array;
L213:     const [a, , b] = array;
L214:     const [a = aDefault, b] = array;
L215:     const [a, b, ...rest] = array;
L216:     const [a, , b, ...rest] = array;
L217:     const [a, b, ...{ pop, push }] = array;
L218:     const [a, b, ...[c, d]] = array;
L219: 
L220:     const { a, b } = obj;
L221:     const { a: a1, b: b1 } = obj;
L222:     const { a: a1 = aDefault, b = bDefault } = obj;
L223:     const { a, b, ...rest } = obj;
L224:     const { a: a1, b: b1, ...rest } = obj;
L225:     const { [key]: a } = obj;
L226:     let a, b, a1, b1, c, d, rest, pop, push;
L227:     [a, b] = array;
L228:     [a, , b] = array;
L229:     [a = aDefault, b] = array;
L230:     [a, b, ...rest] = array;
L231:     [a, , b, ...rest] = array;
L232:     [a, b, ...{ pop, push }] = array;
L233:     [a, b, ...[c, d]] = array;
L234: 
L235:     ({ a, b } = obj); // parentheses are required
L236:     ({ a: a1, b: b1 } = obj);
L237:     ({ a: a1 = aDefault, b = bDefault } = obj);
L238:     ({ a, b, ...rest } = obj);
L239:     ({ a: a1, b: b1, ...rest } = obj);
L240:     `
L241: ## 【90†Description】
L242: 
L243: The object and array literal expressions provide an easy way to create ad hoc packages of data.
L244: 
L245: js
L246: 
L247:     `const arr = [a, b, c];
L248:     `
L249: 
L250: The destructuring uses similar syntax but uses it on the left-hand side of the assignment instead. It performs the reverse operation of an array declaration, by declaring each element in the collection as a separate variable.
L251: 
L252: js
L253: 
L254:     `const arr = [1, 2, 3];
L255:     const [a, b, c] = arr;
L256:     // a = 1, b = 2, c = 3
L257:     `
L258: As for objects, compare the two pairs of lines below, and see how there's a direct correspondence within each pair.
L259: 
L260: js
L261: 
L262:     `const obj = { a, b, c };
L263:     const { a, b, c } = obj;
L264:     // Equivalent to:
L265:     // const a = obj.a, b = obj.b, c = obj.c;
L266: 
L267:     const obj = { prop1: x, prop2: y, prop3: z };
L268:     const { prop1: x, prop2: y, prop3: z } = obj;
L269:     // Equivalent to:
L270:     // const x = obj.prop1, y = obj.prop2, z = obj.prop3;
L271:     `
L272: This capability is similar to features present in languages such as Perl and Python.
L273: 
L274: For features specific to array or object destructuring, refer to the individual 【91†examples】 below.
L275: ### 【94†Binding and assignment】
L276: 
L277: For both object and array destructuring, there are two kinds of destructuring patterns: 【95†binding】 pattern and assignment pattern, with slightly different syntaxes.
L278: 
L279: In binding patterns, the pattern starts with a declaration keyword (`var`, `let`, or `const`). Then, each individual property must either be bound to a variable or further destructured.
L280: js
L281: 
L282:     `const obj = { a: 1, b: { c: 2 } };
L283:     const {
L284:       a,
L285:       b: { c: d },
L286:     } = obj;
L287:     // Two variables are bound: `a` and `d`
L288:     `
L289: 
L290: All variables share the same declaration, so if you want some variables to be re-assignable but others to be read-only, you may have to destructure twice — once with `let`, once with `const`.
L291: 
L292: js
L293: 
L294:     `const obj = { a: 1, b: { c: 2 } };
L295:     const { a } = obj; // a is constant
L296:     let {
L297:       b: { c: d },
L298:     } = obj; // d is re-assignable
L299:     `
L300: In many other syntaxes where the language binds a variable for you, you can use a binding destructuring pattern. These include:
L301: 
L302:   * The looping variable of 【96†`for...in`】, 【97†`for...of`】, and 【98†`for await...of`】 loops;
L303:   * 【33†Function】 parameters;
L304:   * The 【99†`catch`】 binding variable.
L305: In assignment patterns, the pattern does not start with a keyword. Each destructured property is assigned to a target of assignment — which may either be declared beforehand with `var` or `let`, or is a property of another object — in general, anything that can appear on the left-hand side of an assignment expression.
L306: js
L307: 
L308:     `const numbers = [];
L309:     const obj = { a: 1, b: 2 };
L310:     ({ a: numbers[0], b: numbers[1] } = obj);
L311:     // The properties `a` and `b` are assigned to properties of `numbers`
L312:     `
L313: 
L314: Note: The parentheses `( ... )` around the assignment statement are required when using object literal destructuring without a declaration.
L315: `{ a, b } = { a: 1, b: 2 }` is not valid stand-alone syntax, as the `{ a, b }` on the left-hand side is considered a block and not an object literal according to the rules of 【100†expression statements】. However, `({ a, b } = { a: 1, b: 2 })` is valid, as is `const { a, b } = { a: 1, b: 2 }`.
L316: 
L317: If your coding style does not include trailing semicolons, the `( ... )` expression needs to be preceded by a semicolon, or it may be used to execute a function on the previous line.
L318: Note that the equivalent binding pattern of the code above is not valid syntax:
L319: 
L320: js
L321: 
L322:     `const numbers = [];
L323:     const obj = { a: 1, b: 2 };
L324:     const { a: numbers[0], b: numbers[1] } = obj;
L325: 
L326:     // This is equivalent to:
L327:     //   const numbers[0] = obj.a;
L328:     //   const numbers[1] = obj.b;
L329:     // Which definitely is not valid.
L330:     `
L331: You can only use assignment patterns as the left-hand side of the 【101†assignment】 operator. You cannot use them with compound assignment operators such as `+=` or `*=`.
L332: ### 【102†Default value】
L333: 
L334: Each destructured property can have a default value. The default value is used when the property is not present, or has value `undefined`. It is not used if the property has value `null`.
L335: 
L336: js
L337: 
L338:     `const [a = 1] = []; // a is 1
L339:     const { b = 2 } = { b: undefined }; // b is 2
L340:     const { c = 2 } = { c: null }; // c is null
L341:     `
L342: 
L343: The default value can be any expression. It will only be evaluated when necessary.
L344: js
L345: 
L346:     `const { b = console.log("hey") } = { b: 2 };
L347:     // Does not log anything, because `b` is defined and there's no need
L348:     // to evaluate the default value.
L349:     `
L350: ### 【103†Rest properties and rest elements】
L351: 
L352: You can end a destructuring pattern with a rest property `...rest`. For array destructuring, it collects remaining elements of the iterable into a new array called `rest` (or any name you give it). For object destructuring, it copies all enumerable own properties of the object that are not already picked off by the destructuring pattern into a new object called `rest`.
L353: More formally, the `...rest` syntax is called "rest elements" in array destructuring and "rest properties" in object destructuring, but we often just collectively call them "rest property".
L354: 
L355: js
L356: 
L357:     `const { a, ...others } = { a: 1, b: 2, c: 3 };
L358:     console.log(others); // { b: 2, c: 3 }
L359: 
L360:     const [first, ...others2] = [1, 2, 3];
L361:     console.log(others2); // [2, 3]
L362:     `
L363: 
L364: The rest property must be the last in the pattern, and must not have a trailing comma.
L365: js
L366: 
L367:     `const [a, ...b,] = [1, 2, 3];
L368: 
L369:     // SyntaxError: rest element may not have a trailing comma
L370:     // Always consider using rest operator as the last element
L371:     `
L372: 
L373: Like any other JavaScript language feature, there is no implicit deep-copying. The rest property creates a new object (or array), but all its member values, if they are object references, remain the same.
L374: ## 【91†Examples】
L375: 
L376: ### 【104†Array destructuring】
L377: 
L378: #### Basic variable assignment
L379: 
L380: js
L381: 
L382:     `const foo = ["one", "two", "three"];
L383: 
L384:     const [red, yellow, green] = foo;
L385:     console.log(red); // "one"
L386:     console.log(yellow); // "two"
L387:     console.log(green); // "three"
L388:     `
L389: #### Destructuring with more elements than the source
L390: 
L391: In an array destructuring from an array of length N specified on the right-hand side of the assignment, if the number of variables specified on the left-hand side of the assignment is greater than N, only the first N variables are assigned values. The values of the remaining variables will be undefined.
L392: js
L393: 
L394:     `const foo = ["one", "two"];
L395: 
L396:     const [red, yellow, green, blue] = foo;
L397:     console.log(red); // "one"
L398:     console.log(yellow); // "two"
L399:     console.log(green); // undefined
L400:     console.log(blue); // undefined
L401:     `
L402: #### Swapping variables
L403: 
L404: You can swap the values of two variables in one destructuring expression.
L405: 
L406: Without destructuring, swapping two values requires a temporary variable (or, in some low-level languages, the 【105†XOR-swap trick†en.wikipedia.org】).
L407: 
L408: js
L409: 
L410:     `let a = 1;
L411:     let b = 3;
L412: 
L413:     [a, b] = [b, a];
L414:     console.log(a); // 3
L415:     console.log(b); // 1
L416: 
L417:     const arr = [1, 2, 3];
L418:     [arr[2], arr[1]] = [arr[1], arr[2]];
L419:     console.log(arr); // [1, 3, 2]
L420:     `
L421: #### Parsing an array returned from a function
L422: 
L423: It's always been possible to return an array from a function. Destructuring can make working with an array return value more concise.
L424: 
L425: In this example, `f()` returns the values `[1, 2]` as its output, which can be parsed in a single line with destructuring.
L426: 
L427: js
L428: 
L429:     `function f() {
L430:       return [1, 2];
L431:     }
L432: 
L433:     const [a, b] = f();
L434:     console.log(a); // 1
L435:     console.log(b); // 2
L436:     `
L437: #### Ignoring some returned values
L438: 
L439: You can ignore return values that you're not interested in:
L440: 
L441: js
L442: 
L443:     `function f() {
L444:       return [1, 2, 3];
L445:     }
L446: 
L447:     const [a, , b] = f();
L448:     console.log(a); // 1
L449:     console.log(b); // 3
L450: 
L451:     const [c] = f();
L452:     console.log(c); // 1
L453:     `
L454: 
L455: You can also ignore all returned values:
L456: 
L457: js
L458: 
L459:     `[, ,] = f();
L460:     `
L461: Though in this case, it's probably clearer to just call the function and not use destructuring at all. You don't have to use the return value.
L462: #### Using a binding pattern as the rest property
L463: 
L464: The rest property of array destructuring can be another array or object binding pattern. The inner destructuring destructures from the array created after collecting the rest elements, so you cannot access any properties present on the original iterable in this way.
L465: 
L466: js
L467: 
L468:     `const [a, b, ...{ length }] = [1, 2, 3];
L469:     console.log(a, b, length); // 1 2 1
L470:     `
L471: js
L472: 
L473:     `const [a, b, ...[c, d]] = [1, 2, 3, 4];
L474:     console.log(a, b, c, d); // 1 2 3 4
L475:     `
L476: 
L477: These binding patterns can even be nested, as long as each rest property is the last in the list.
L478: 
L479: js
L480: 
L481:     `const [a, b, ...[c, d, ...[e, f]]] = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6];
L482:     console.log(a, b, c, d, e, f); // 1 2 3 4 5 6
L483:     `
L484: 
L485: On the other hand, object destructuring can only have an identifier (or a property access in assignment patterns) as the rest property.
L486: js
L487: 
L488:     `const { a, ...{ b } } = { a: 1, b: 2 };
L489:     // SyntaxError: `...` must be followed by an identifier in declaration contexts
L490: 
L491:     let a, b;
L492:     ({ a, ...{ b } } = { a: 1, b: 2 });
L493:     // SyntaxError: `...` must be followed by an assignable reference in assignment contexts
L494:     `
L495: #### Unpacking values from a regular expression match
L496: 
L497: When the regular expression 【106†`exec()`】 method finds a match, it returns an array containing first the entire matched portion of the string and then the portions of the string that matched each parenthesized group in the regular expression. Destructuring allows you to unpack the parts out of this array easily, ignoring the full match if it is not needed.
L498: js
L499: 
L500:     `function parseProtocol(url) {
L501:       const parsedURL = /^(\w+):\/\/([^/]+)\/(.*)$/.exec(url);
L502:       if (!parsedURL) {
L503:         return false;
L504:       }
L505:       console.log(parsedURL);
L506:       // ["https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript",
L507:       // "https", "developer.mozilla.org", "en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript"]
L508: 
L509:       const [, protocol, fullHost, fullPath] = parsedURL;
L510:       return protocol;
L511:     }
L512: 
L513:     console.log(
L514:       parseProtocol("https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript"),
L515:     );
L516:     // "https"
L517:     `
L518: #### Using array destructuring on any iterable
L519: 
L520: Array destructuring calls the 【107†iterable protocol】 of the right-hand side. Therefore, any iterable, not necessarily arrays, can be destructured.
L521: 
L522: js
L523: 
L524:     `const [a, b] = new Map([
L525:       [1, 2],
L526:       [3, 4],
L527:     ]);
L528:     console.log(a, b); // [1, 2] [3, 4]
L529:     `
L530: 
L531: Non-iterables cannot be destructured as arrays.
L532: 
L533: js
L534: 
L535:     `const obj = { 0: "a", 1: "b", length: 2 };
L536:     const [a, b] = obj;
L537:     // TypeError: obj is not iterable
L538:     `
L539: Iterables are only iterated until all bindings are assigned.
L540: 
L541: js
L542: 
L543:     `const obj = {
L544:       *[Symbol.iterator]() {
L545:         for (const v of [0, 1, 2, 3]) {
L546:           console.log(v);
L547:           yield v;
L548:         }
L549:       },
L550:     };
L551:     const [a, b] = obj; // Only logs 0 and 1
L552:     `
L553: 
L554: The rest binding is eagerly evaluated and creates a new array, instead of using the old iterable.
L555: js
L556: 
L557:     `const obj = {
L558:       *[Symbol.iterator]() {
L559:         for (const v of [0, 1, 2, 3]) {
L560:           console.log(v);
L561:           yield v;
L562:         }
L563:       },
L564:     };
L565:     const [a, b, ...rest] = obj; // Logs 0 1 2 3
L566:     console.log(rest); // [2, 3] (an array)
L567:     `
L568: ### 【108†Object destructuring】
L569: 
L570: #### Basic assignment
L571: 
L572: js
L573: 
L574:     `const user = {
L575:       id: 42,
L576:       isVerified: true,
L577:     };
L578: 
L579:     const { id, isVerified } = user;
L580: 
L581:     console.log(id); // 42
L582:     console.log(isVerified); // true
L583:     `
L584: #### Assigning to new variable names
L585: 
L586: A property can be unpacked from an object and assigned to a variable with a different name than the object property.
L587: 
L588: js
L589: 
L590:     `const o = { p: 42, q: true };
L591:     const { p: foo, q: bar } = o;
L592: 
L593:     console.log(foo); // 42
L594:     console.log(bar); // true
L595:     `
L596: 
L597: Here, for example, `const { p: foo } = o` takes from the object `o` the property named `p` and assigns it to a local variable named `foo`.
L598: #### Assigning to new variable names and providing default values
L599: 
L600: A property can be both
L601: 
L602:   * Unpacked from an object and assigned to a variable with a different name.
L603:   * Assigned a default value in case the unpacked value is `undefined`.
L604: 
L605: js
L606: 
L607:     `const { a: aa = 10, b: bb = 5 } = { a: 3 };
L608: 
L609:     console.log(aa); // 3
L610:     console.log(bb); // 5
L611:     `
L612: #### Unpacking properties from objects passed as a function parameter
L613: 
L614: Objects passed into function parameters can also be unpacked into variables, which may then be accessed within the function body. As for object assignment, the destructuring syntax allows for the new variable to have the same name or a different name than the original property, and to assign default values for the case when the original object does not define the property.
L615: 
L616: Consider this object, which contains information about a user.
L617: js
L618: 
L619:     `const user = {
L620:       id: 42,
L621:       displayName: "jdoe",
L622:       fullName: {
L623:         firstName: "Jane",
L624:         lastName: "Doe",
L625:       },
L626:     };
L627:     `
L628: 
L629: Here we show how to unpack a property of the passed object into a variable with the same name. The parameter value `{ id }` indicates that the `id` property of the object passed to the function should be unpacked into a variable with the same name, which can then be used within the function.
L630: js
L631: 
L632:     `function userId({ id }) {
L633:       return id;
L634:     }
L635: 
L636:     console.log(userId(user)); // 42
L637:     `
L638: 
L639: You can define the name of the unpacked variable. Here we unpack the property named `displayName`, and rename it to `dname` for use within the function body.
L640: 
L641: js
L642: 
L643:     `function userDisplayName({ displayName: dname }) {
L644:       return dname;
L645:     }
L646: 
L647:     console.log(userDisplayName(user)); // "jdoe"
L648:     `
L649: Nested objects can also be unpacked. The example below shows the property `fullName.firstName` being unpacked into a variable called `name`.
L650: 
L651: js
L652: 
L653:     `function whois({ displayName, fullName: { firstName: name } }) {
L654:       return `${displayName} is ${name}`;
L655:     }
L656: 
L657:     console.log(whois(user)); // "jdoe is Jane"
L658:     `
L659: #### Setting a function parameter's default value
L660: 
L661: Default values can be specified using `=`, and will be used as variable values if a specified property does not exist in the passed object.
L662: 
L663: Below we show a function where the default size is `'big'`, default co-ordinates are `x: 0, y: 0` and default radius is 25.
L664: js
L665: 
L666:     `function drawChart({
L667:       size = "big",
L668:       coords = { x: 0, y: 0 },
L669:       radius = 25,
L670:     } = {}) {
L671:       console.log(size, coords, radius);
L672:       // do some chart drawing
L673:     }
L674: 
L675:     drawChart({
L676:       coords: { x: 18, y: 30 },
L677:       radius: 30,
L678:     });
L679:     `
L680: 
L681: In the function signature for `drawChart` above, the destructured left-hand side has a default value of an empty object `= {}`.
L682: You could have also written the function without that default. However, if you leave out that default value, the function will look for at least one argument to be supplied when invoked, whereas in its current form, you can call `drawChart()` without supplying any parameters. Otherwise, you need to at least supply an empty object literal.
L683: 
L684: For more information, see 【109†Default parameters > Destructured parameter with default value assignment】.
L685: #### Nested object and array destructuring
L686: js
L687: 
L688:     `const metadata = {
L689:       title: "Scratchpad",
L690:       translations: [
L691:         {
L692:           locale: "de",
L693:           localizationTags: [],
L694:           lastEdit: "2014-04-14T08:43:37",
L695:           url: "/de/docs/Tools/Scratchpad",
L696:           title: "JavaScript-Umgebung",
L697:         },
L698:       ],
L699:       url: "/en-US/docs/Tools/Scratchpad",
L700:     };
L701: 
L702:     const {
L703:       title: englishTitle, // rename
L704:       translations: [
L705:         {
L706:           title: localeTitle, // rename
L707:         },
L708:       ],
L709:     } = metadata;
L710: 
L711:     console.log(englishTitle); // "Scratchpad"
L712:     console.log(localeTitle); // "JavaScript-Umgebung"
L713:     `
